questions.question: Using the key numbers, describe South Africa's rainfall in space and in time, and explain how evaporation and the runoff ratio shrink the national water budget.
questions.expected_answer: South Africa averages about 465 millimetres of rain a year against a world average of about 860 — a little more than half the world's ration. In space the rain slides from east to west: the eastern escarpment and KwaZulu-Natal coast receive over 1 000 millimetres, the central plateau 400 to 600, the Karoo and Namaqualand under 200, and the desert coast near the Orange mouth under 50, with roughly two thirds of the country below the 500-millimetre threshold for rain-fed cropping. In time the rain is seasonal — summer thunderstorm rain over the interior and east, winter frontal rain in the south-western Cape, all-season rain only on a narrow southern coastal strip — and unreliable between years, with the percentage swings growing wilder toward the west. Evaporation then taxes the budget: over most of the interior the atmosphere could lift more water off an open surface in a year than the sky delivers, exceeding 2 500 millimetres of potential loss in parts of the Northern Cape, so every dam and pan constantly loses water. The result is the runoff ratio: only about 9 per cent of South Africa's rainfall ever becomes river flow, the rest being evaporated, transpired or soaked beyond reach — and most of the flow that can be affordably captured already has been.

questions.question: Classify South Africa's rivers as perennial, periodic and episodic, naming examples, and explain both the pattern this classification draws across the country and the exception the Orange River represents.
questions.expected_answer: A perennial river flows every day of the year, sustained between rains by groundwater seeping into its channel — the rivers of the well-watered east and south, such as the Thukela dropping off the Drakensberg, the Breede and the Berg. A periodic or non-perennial river flows only during and shortly after the rainy season, the pattern of the drier plateau. An episodic river flows only after occasional heavy storms and may lie dry for years, like the Molopo and Auob on the Kalahari margins. Moving west across the country the types change in exactly the order the rainfall map dictates — perennial, then periodic, then episodic — because the rain thins from over 1 000 millimetres in the east to under 50 in the west. The Orange, or Gariep, is the great exception: born in the Lesotho highlands where rain and snow are abundant, it carries that mountain water about 2 200 kilometres westward through near-desert to the Atlantic at Alexander Bay, so a strong permanent river crosses country that could never have produced one. Its partner the Vaal drains the industrial plateau and supplies Gauteng, which has no major river of its own. South African rivers also run heavy with silt, which settles in dams and shrinks storage, and even perennial rivers swing seasonally, which is why storage is essential.

questions.question: Explain why South Africa relies on built dams and on groundwater rather than natural lakes, and organise the physical and human factors that determine the country's water availability.
questions.expected_answer: Natural lakes need glaciers or rivers with surplus water; South Africa's warm, dry history provided neither, so its few naturals — Fundudzi, the Chrissiesmeer pans, coastal lakes like Sibaya — are famous exceptions. Instead the country built over 500 large dams storing about two thirds of mean annual runoff: the Gariep, the largest, with Vanderkloof regulating the Orange for irrigation and power; the Vaal Dam as Gauteng's tank; Sterkfontein as the pumped strategic reserve held for drought; Theewaterskloof supplying Cape Town, whose 2018 near-emptiness produced Day Zero; Midmar and Jozini serving KwaZulu-Natal. Dams pay two taxes — fierce evaporation off the top and silt filling the bottom. Groundwater in aquifers is the third source, hidden from the sun and available beneath riverless districts — the boreholes and windpumps of the Karoo, the dolomite aquifers of Gauteng and North West — but over-pumping lowers the water table and seeped pollution such as acid mine drainage is nearly permanent. The physical factors behind availability are rainfall amount (465 against 860), its east-west distribution, seasonality and year-to-year variability, evaporation exceeding rainfall over the interior, relief and geology deciding dam sites and aquifers, and the 9 per cent runoff ratio. The human factors are the mismatch of people and water, with Gauteng on a dry watershed; rising demand led by irrigation at roughly 60 per cent; pollution from sewage failures, industry and acid mine drainage; thirsty alien invasive plants; leaking municipal systems losing a third or more as non-revenue water; and the quality of management itself.
